questions.prompt: What main claim does Chapter 9 make about big goals?
choices: Large goals are automatically reckless
Big is not automatically bad when the scale is legitimate
Only small goals can be realistic

explanation.gentle: The chapter rejects default suspicion of size.
explanation.direct: Keller says scale itself is not the real problem.
explanation.competitive: Large is not guilty by default.

questions.prompt: Why does Keller treat size aversion as a lie?
choices: Because people often confuse comfort with wisdom when sizing goals
Because every large goal is smarter than every small one
Because risk never matters

explanation.gentle: The chapter says smaller can feel wiser mainly because it disturbs less.
explanation.competitive: Comfort often wins the sizing fight and gets called maturity.

questions.prompt: What does comfort-sized ambition mean in this chapter?
choices: Lowering the goal until it fits life with less disruption
Choosing a goal with more detail and sequence
Waiting until a goal becomes emotionally exciting

explanation.gentle: The chapter uses this phrase for shrinking a goal so it feels easier to carry.
explanation.direct: The target gets resized for ease more than truth.
explanation.competitive: The goal gets cut until it stops demanding much.

questions.prompt: Talia sees a team keep trimming a meaningful target because the bigger version feels exposed. What best fits Chapter 9?
choices: Keep reducing it until nobody feels stretched
Protect the larger grounded version if comfort is the real reason for cutting it down
Treat any ambitious target as ego by default

explanation.gentle: The chapter says a larger goal should not be cut down automatically if it is still real.
explanation.direct: Do not mistake discomfort for proof against scale.
explanation.competitive: If the target is real, stop letting comfort shave it down.

questions.prompt: Which statement would Chapter 9 reject as false?
choices: A grounded large aim can be legitimate
Smaller goals are always wiser because they disturb less
Big is not automatically bad

explanation.gentle: The chapter rejects the idea that smaller is automatically wiser.
explanation.direct: Less disturbance is not enough to prove better judgment.
explanation.competitive: Easy on comfort is not the same as true.

questions.prompt: Marcus lowered his project standard before he even tested whether the stronger version was possible. What did Chapter 9 say he missed?
choices: The value of adding more research citations
The need to make every goal larger than possible
The difference between prudence and comfort-sized retreat

explanation.gentle: He may have reduced the standard for comfort before judging it fairly.
explanation.direct: The chapter asks whether the smaller goal was wiser or just safer.
explanation.competitive: He may have called relief realism.

questions.prompt: What limit keeps Chapter 9 from becoming grandiosity?
choices: Only work goals can be large
Any bigger goal is automatically justified
A large aim still has to stay grounded and real

explanation.gentle: The chapter does not defend fantasy. It defends legitimate scale.
explanation.competitive: If the target is inflated theater, it still fails.

questions.prompt: Ren keeps rewriting a life aim into smaller versions that feel easier to carry without changing much. What is the best Chapter 9 response?
choices: The smaller version is automatically more mature
Any larger version would obviously be fantasy
That pattern may show comfort deciding size more than truth

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns that practical-sounding reductions can hide comfort.
explanation.direct: A smaller life aim may be serving relief rather than judgment.
explanation.competitive: The respectable rewrite may be the retreat.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 9 build on Chapter 8?
choices: It explains why people sometimes choose smaller goals to avoid the visible tilt a bigger goal would create
It says balance no longer matters because ambition replaces it
It replaces tradeoffs with emotional confidence

explanation.gentle: Chapter 8 exposed fear of imbalance, and Chapter 9 shows how that fear can shrink ambition.
explanation.direct: The smaller goal can be a way to avoid the season the bigger goal would demand.
explanation.competitive: People cut the target down so life never has to confess a real tilt.

questions.prompt: Which action best applies Chapter 9 to a crowded life?
choices: Assume the smaller version of every goal is wiser
Keep the goal as large as truth requires while rejecting fantasy
Choose the biggest possible target so you never look timid

explanation.gentle: The chapter works when scale is sized by truth instead of by comfort or ego.
explanation.direct: Defend legitimate scale and reject empty inflation.
explanation.competitive: Do not cut for relief or swell for show. Size it honestly.
